title: Just Keep Swimming: Benchmarking OSS Agent Memory on Kubernetes with OpenTelemetry
tldr: Henrik Rexed benchmarks five open-source agent memory servers on kagent with a shared generic MCP layer and OpenTelemetry instrumentation he contributed upstream. Memory helps only when recall is precise: embedding and graph approaches did best for SRE investigations, a key-based store did best for context-rich coding crews, and MemPalace and Zep were the most consistent overall.

key_points.text: Agents without memory repeat investigations and tool calls they already did, wasting tools and tokens; memory servers let agents store and recall facts.

Architectures range from pure embeddings, to vector plus graph, knowledge graphs, temporal knowledge graphs, and a key/metadata store plus vector and graph (MemKeys, the speaker's own two-week-old project).
Common layers: ingest and search paths, an optional LLM to embed and categorize facts, graph building done asynchronously, and usually an MCP server for agent access.
MemPalace organizes memory into wings per project and drawers per category; Zep (Graphiti) tracks when facts change so it can answer what was true before and now.

Harness: kagent agents on DeepSeek, a generic MCP for add, search, get, update and delete so only the backend changes, and OpenTelemetry instrumentation contributed to each backend (some PRs were rejected, so forks were used).

Scenario 1: an SRE agent diagnoses Kubernetes failures (CrashLoopBackOff, ImagePullBackOff, OOM kills, pending pods) and bad Gateway API and GAMMA gRPC route configs, measured as warm minus cold runs.
Scenario 2: a BMAD-method crew over A2A builds an expense approval app, is stopped mid-feature and resumed, then gets a fact change (PostgreSQL to MySQL).
Memory raises input tokens, though these may be billed as cached input; retrieving too many or wrong facts confuses the LLM and makes results worse.
SRE results: MemOS, Zep and MemPalace improved with memory; Mem0 and MemKeys got worse, with MemKeys pulling far too many facts.
Coding crew results: the key store did best on build, resume and restart, using far fewer tokens because tasks carry rich context; MemPalace and Zep also did well.
Few backends offer a UI to inspect stored memory, which matters for pruning noise that degrades search.

numbers.text: Memory server footprint was around 250 to 300 MB.
MemKeys used about 55 millicores of CPU on retrieval in the SRE scenario.
In the coding scenario MemKeys used about 20 millicores more than the others.
Add and search latencies were on the scale of a few microseconds, up to about 20 microseconds.
The other projects have more than 10K GitHub stars; MemKeys has zero.

open_gaps.text: Most memory backends do not ship OpenTelemetry support, and some maintainers rejected upstream PRs because telemetry is a commercial feature.
Memory scoping and isolation between users or channels was not evaluated, and the speaker did not know which backends support it.
Several earlier candidates (Cognee, Memu, Honcho) were dropped over licensing changes, and other popular tools are not yet covered.
Adding a backend to the benchmark is laborious: MCP connectivity, OpenTelemetry instrumentation, then scenario design.

opportunities.text: Add OpenTelemetry instrumentation for ingest and recall operations to open-source memory servers.
Measure agent memory as warm-run minus cold-run tokens and tool calls on your own workloads before adopting a backend.
Test whether memory backends isolate recall by user or channel before using them in shared bots.
Compare embedding, temporal knowledge graph and key-indexed memory designs against SRE-style versus project-style agent tasks.
